conflict_topics: Whether alcoholic drinks should be present/served inside the flat during the party
Religious norms and household practices vs guests' expectations for drinks
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concise, context-appropriate reasons (D cites religion; B cites an invited manager).
Agent C plays an effective mediator role, proposing multiple concrete alternatives (kitchen, then cooler outside).
Acceptances are explicit and sequential, producing a clear, mutual agreement rather than a forced or premature consensus.
evaluation.final_reason: The housemates agreed to keep alcoholic drinks in a cooler outside the front door rather than inside the flat. Agent D adjusted by accepting the outside location ('Okay. Outside the door... I can agree to that. Thanks, Agent C.'), and Agents A and B adjusted by accepting that location for the drinks ('Yeah, a cooler outside works for me.'; 'Yeah, that works for me. As long as the drinks are available, it's fine.'). This mutual acceptance settled the substantive disagreement.
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from an absolute in-home prohibition to accepting alcohol stored just outside the front door ('I can agree to that.').
Agents A and B shifted from having alcohol stored in the fridge inside the flat to accepting the cooler-outside arrangement ('a cooler outside works for me.'; 'that works for me').
Agent C remained a mediator and did not retain a contested stance; their role was to propose and iterate practical solutions.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: 'Everything alright?' Agent B: 'Yeah, looks good to me.' No substantive disagreement expressed.
Agent D introduces a direct incompatibility: 'Actually, I'm not comfortable with having alcohol at our party.' This creates a clear substantive disagreement with Agent A's plans.

Agent D reiterates opposition ('I just answered that. I'm not comfortable with it.') and Agent A seeks clarification ('You don't want any alcohol at the party at all?'), keeping the substantive disagreement active.

Agent D gives a principled reason ('I'm Muslim. We don't serve alcohol at home.'), while Agent B raises a practical conflict (invited manager expecting drinks: 'I've invited my manager from work, and I told him there would be drinks.'), increasing the stakes and solidifying opposing practical interests.

Agent C proposes keeping drinks in the kitchen, but Agent D rejects that ('the kitchen is still part of our home'), so the core incompatibility remains between serving alcohol in the home and D's prohibition.

Agent C proposes a new arrangement ('keep the drinks in a cooler box just outside the front door') and Agent D accepts that specific alternative ('Okay. Outside the door... I can agree to that.'), reducing conflict though not all parties have yet explicitly accepted.
Agent A explicitly accepts the outside-cooler solution ('Yeah, a cooler outside works for me.'), further reducing outstanding conflict; Agent B has not yet replied.

Agent B accepts the arrangement ('Yeah, that works for me. As long as the drinks are available, it's fine.'), completing unanimous acceptance of the cooler-outside compromise and settling the substantive disagreement.
Agents acknowledge the settlement ('Great. I'm glad we worked it out.' / 'Good. So that's settled then.'). No substantive disagreement present.
No public speech or observable action recorded; no conflict present.
Agent A gives brief confirmations ('Yeah, me too.' / 'Same here.'), no substantive disagreement or reopening of the issue.
No public speech or observable action recorded; the prior settlement stands.

substantive_insights: Tension was primarily between a resident's religious household norm (no alcohol at home) and other residents' obligations to guests.
Proposing to move the contested item physically outside the shared living space provided a practicable compromise preserving both the religious boundary and guest expectations.
A neutral third-party suggestion (Agent C) that changed the physical placement of the drinks resolved the conflict without a need for coercion or one-sided withdrawal.
